beats.prose:
The salvage scanner pinged—another piece of corporate debris, solar panel still half-functional, tumbling at point-three rotations per minute. Kael marked the coordinates and moved on. The Iron Ghost's bridge hummed with the soft, predictable voice of a ship that had learned to keep its complaints quiet. Seven years of this. Seven years of the same: scan, catalog, strip, sell the components to independent stations that paid cash and asked no questions.

He ran a hand across the navigation console, fingers trailing over the worn plastic where the previous owner's name had been scratched away. His own name was nowhere on this ship. Just the call sign, Iron Ghost, stenciled in fading white on the hull. Fitting. A ghost that salvaged other ghosts.

The neural implant twitched. Not pain exactly—the implant didn't do pain, not anymore—but a stuttering in the signal, like static bleeding through from somewhere very far away. Kael closed his eyes. The screams were there again, buried under seven years of deliberate numbness, waiting in the spaces between his heartbeats. He could hear them if he let himself listen. Hale's voice, thin and fractured as ice. The sound his own voice made when he pulled the trigger.

He opened his eyes and pushed the sensation down. Routine. That was the word. That was the answer to everything that threatened to surface.

The scanner picked up another signal—this one old, encrypted, with a timestamp that didn't make sense. Kael leaned forward. The beacon wasn't broadcasting any corporate signature, wasn't broadcasting anything modern. The encryption was clean but ancient, the kind of thing you'd find in a time capsule or a grave.

He should ignore it. Ignored signals were what kept salvage operators alive.

He punched in the coordinates anyway.

The scanner's resolution sharpened as Kael locked onto the signal. Not a reflection. Not solar noise. Something solid, something deliberate, sending out a pulse every 4.3 seconds with the precision of a heartbeat that had been beating for a very long time.

He pulled up the spectral analysis. The signal wasn't broadcasting in any frequency the Five used. Wasn't broadcasting in any frequency anyone used anymore. The encryption layers peeled back like old skin—ancient, but not dead. Still alive. Still calling.

The coordinates resolved into a bearing two degrees below the ecliptic, fifteen million kilometers out from his current drift. Deep enough that the corporate networks would have maybe three seconds of visibility before the signal dropped below their sensor ceiling. Deep enough that no patrol would bother following.

Kael sat back. The Iron Ghost's bridge felt smaller than it had an hour ago.

He should kill the scanner. Mark the bearing as junk and move on. Salvage operators who chased unknown signals ended up as unknown signals themselves—derelicts drifting in the black with no one left to mark their coordinates. The rule was simple: you don't go toward the things you don't understand. You go away from them.

The pulse came again. 4.3 seconds. 4.3 seconds. Like something waiting.

Like something that knew he was listening.

Kael's hand moved across the navigation console before the thought had fully formed. Course plotting. Fuel burn calculations. The Iron Ghost would take forty hours to reach those coordinates at cruise, another six to brake hard enough not to overshoot into the void. Forty-six hours. Forty-six hours of that pulse counting down in his neural implant, getting louder, getting clearer.

Forty-six hours for curiosity to kill him.

He engaged the drive. The ship groaned—the sound of old metal accepting one more burden it wasn't built for—and the stars began to slide across the viewscreen. Behind him, the scanner kept its rhythm. In his skull, the implant echoed it back: a signal calling to a signal, one ghost reaching out to another across the frozen dark.

Kael didn't question it. He'd learned long ago that questioning was another way of staying alive. And staying alive, he'd discovered, was just another way of staying alone.

The shape resolved out of the darkness forty-six hours later, and Kael's breath caught in his throat—a rare thing, rarer still for a man who'd trained the reflex out of himself years ago.

Eight hundred meters of sleek black crystal, matte and seamless, rotating slowly on an axis that had nothing to do with momentum. Faint bioluminescent runes pulsed along its surface in patterns that hurt to look at directly, as if his eyes kept trying to find meaning in mathematics they couldn't parse. The hull was intact. Perfect. Impossible.

Not human. Not corporate. Not anything that belonged in a solar system the Five had spent sixty years cataloging and claiming.

Kael cut the Iron Ghost's engines and let her drift. The scanner painted the shape in slow, methodical sweeps. No heat signature. No power emissions. No radiation except the soft, steady pulse of those runes—a heartbeat that had been beating, he understood with a cold certainty that settled behind his ribs, for a very long time.

Millennia, maybe. Longer.

His hand moved across the console to engage the suit-up sequence before the thought had fully formed. The pressure suit hung in the locker like shed skin, and he pulled it on with the mechanical precision of someone performing a ritual he'd performed ten thousand times. Seal the seams. Check the readouts. Trust the systems because the only alternative was to trust himself to improvise at vacuum pressure, and no one improvised well at vacuum pressure.

The airlock cycled. The void swallowed him.

The crossing took twenty minutes. Twenty minutes of firing the suit's maneuvering thrusters in short, controlled bursts, watching the crystalline hull grow larger with each meter closed. The runes didn't glow brighter as he approached—they maintained their slow, patient pulse, indifferent to his presence.

Until his gloved hand touched the hull.

Warmth. That was the first thing—impossible, absolute warmth radiating through the suit's thermal layers as if the ship's very substance was alive and aware and had been waiting for a hand exactly like his to make contact. The second thing was the signal. Not in his ears. Not in the suit's radio. In his skull. In the neural implant behind his left temple, the one that had resisted the Europa wipe when it should have shattered like every other brain in that lab.

Recognition.

Not welcome. Not hostile. Recognition. As if the ship had been waiting for someone with his particular signature—someone whose implant had already touched the edge of something ancient and survived.

Kael's breath came shallow in his helmet. The void pressed against the suit's fabric with the weight of seven years of isolation, and he understood, in that moment of absolute clarity, that he had crossed a threshold that had no return on the other side.

The airlock was somewhere behind him. The Iron Ghost was a diminishing point of light. Forty-six hours of careful distance had just been annihilated by a single warm touch.

He pulled himself toward the hull's entrance—a seam that opened like an eye recognizing him—and the darkness of the ship swallowed him whole.

The airlock sealed behind him with a sound like a closing eyelid, and the darkness inside the probe was absolute—not the darkness of space, which at least had stars, but the darkness of something sealed against time itself. His suit lights carved white tunnels through the black, and they seemed to dissolve after only a few meters, as if the interior was too vast for light to reach the far side.

He moved deeper. Breathing steady. Heart steady. The lies he told himself every morning held firm.

The chamber opened without warning, and Kael's breath stuttered.

It wasn't empty. It was full—but not with debris or wreckage. The interior was a cathedral of crystalline structures suspended in zero-g, floating like frozen fractals of mathematics made solid. They hung at impossible angles, catching his suit lights and throwing them back in colors that didn't exist in nature: deep ultraviolet, infrared visible as ghost-light, colors between the colors. The air itself felt cold and metallic against the suit's exterior, and when he checked the thermal readout, it should have registered as lethal. Instead, the display flickered and stabilized at a temperature that made no sense: exactly 37.2 degrees Celsius. Body temperature. As if the ship had read him on contact and was now breathing at his frequency.

At the chamber's heart, suspended in the absolute center of the void, floated something else.

A device. But device was the wrong word—it was a crystal, perfect and geometric, a shape that seemed to shift between states the longer he looked at it. Square becoming octagon becoming something that had no name in three dimensions. It pulsed with a rhythm that matched nothing except the steady beat of his own heart, and Kael understood with a clarity that bypassed thought entirely that the device was reading him the way the ship had read him. It was waiting. Had been waiting. For someone exactly like him.

He moved toward it without deciding to move.

The crystalline structures parted as he crossed the chamber, creating a corridor of floating geometry that guided him forward. His suit thrusters weren't firing. He was drifting on momentum alone, but his trajectory was perfect—drawn along a line that had been calculated for him before he was born. The device grew larger. Closer. Its pulse synchronized with his breathing. With his heart. With the small, panicked voice in his implant that was screaming something he couldn't quite hear.

Fifty meters. Thirty. Ten.

He reached out. His gloved hand extended toward the crystal, and then—without thinking, without deciding, without any conscious choice that could later be blamed on reason or training—he removed the glove.

The suit's pressure alarm howled in his helmet. Seconds of exposure. Ten at most before hypoxia became irreversible. His fingers were bare and burning cold in the vacuum, the skin already beginning to blister.

He touched the device anyway.

The light was blue and absolute and it came from inside his skull. Not pain. Not quite. It was the sensation of being recognized by something that had been looking for him across millennia, and when it found him, it didn't stop looking. It poured into him—through him—a torrent of data that his neural implant tried and failed to process. Coordinates that burned like brand marks in his visual cortex. Warnings in languages that weren't words but were somehow understood at the cellular level. A countdown. A number that started in the billions and was already moving toward zero with the inevitability of a clock that had been ticking since before his parents' parents were born.

The device didn't bond with him. It fused. The distinction mattered, though he couldn't have said why. Bonding implied two separate things joining. This was integration. Assimilation. The device and the neural implant and Kael Voss himself were no longer three things but one thing wearing three skins.

His gloved hand came back up instinctively, and he looked at the bare fingers—frostbitten, blistered, already turning the color of old meat. He flexed them. Felt nothing. The pain receptors had shut down or he had shut them down, and he couldn't remember which. Behind his eyes, the blue light was fading but not gone. It was settling. Taking root. The countdown was still there, visible in the peripheral edges of his consciousness like a clock he could never quite look directly at.

Billions. Millions. Thousands.

Hours.

He didn't know how long he floated there in the center of the chamber, watching the crystalline structures orbit him in patterns that made sense now in a way they hadn't before. The device—his device, his burden, his sentence—pulsed against his palm. The blue light flickered in the depths of his implant and refused to die.

When he finally turned back toward the airlock, his movements were different. Sharper. More certain. The suit's systems had gone quiet. The pressure alarm had stopped screaming because his body had stopped telling the suit it was dying. He was or wasn't in critical condition anymore. The distinction seemed small.

The airlock was where it had been. He cycled through. The void outside was the same void he had crossed into, but he was not the same man who had crossed it. Seven years of careful isolation, of staying apart and untouched and safe, had ended in a single moment of contact.

The Iron Ghost hung against the stars like a prayer that had already been answered.

He was halfway across the void when the first signal hit the colony on Europa. Three million kilometers away, every neural implant in the research facility went dark in sequence—a cascade of synaptic failure that took four minutes and thirty seconds to complete. By the time Kael's boots touched the Iron Ghost's airlock, there were no more screams coming through the emergency channels. There were no screams at all.

Just static. Just silence. Just the sound of a countdown that only he could hear, ticking down toward something that was already too late to stop.

The knowledge came in layers, each one building on the last like a wave that wouldn't break, only grow.

First: coordinates. Not numbers on a screen but burned directly into his visual cortex, a three-dimensional map that existed in the space behind his eyes. Europa. Titan. The Lagrange points. Ceres. Dozens of locations scattered across the solar system like markers placed by careful, patient hands. Each one pulsed with a frequency he could feel in his teeth.

Then: images. Not visual—something deeper. He saw the probe as it had been before time had any meaning for it, sleek and alive and burning with purpose. He saw the species that had built it, creatures of light and mathematics, moving through the dark with intention that predated human language. He saw them leave their warnings behind like breadcrumbs, like prayers, like a message in a bottle cast into an ocean that wouldn't exist for forty thousand years.

The warning came last, and it came with weight.

Something is awake.

Not words. The meaning arrived fully formed in his consciousness, carved directly into his neural architecture by something that didn't need language to be understood. Something had been sleeping—had been made to sleep by the device itself, by a failsafe that was supposed to hold forever. But failsafes could fail. Seals could crack. And something that had been dormant in the deep dark between the stars was now opening its eyes.

The countdown in his skull accelerated.

Kael gasped. His body was still floating in the chamber, but his consciousness was scattered across light-years, and the two pieces of him weren't syncing properly. His lungs burned. His neural implant was screaming warnings in languages that predated human neurology—his own neural implant, except it wasn't his anymore. The device had integrated too thoroughly. They were the same thing now, and that same thing was dying from the knowledge it was being forced to carry.

He pulled his hand back from the device. The movement felt wrong, like trying to move a limb that had been asleep for years. The bare fingers were still frostbitten, still dying, but they moved. The pain had shut off somewhere between the moment of contact and now. Maybe that was mercy. Maybe that was the device being kind. He couldn't tell anymore what was him and what was the crystalline thing that had fused itself to his consciousness like a second skull.

The chamber tilted.

No—his perception tilted. The structures still orbited in their patient geometric patterns, but now he could see what they really were. Not random fragments. Not decoration. They were a map. A three-dimensional catalog of every location where the signal had been placed. Every point where the failsafe had been anchored. And they were all still broadcasting. All still waiting. All still counting down toward the same inevitable moment.

The vision faded. Not cleanly. It pulled away like water draining, leaving behind only the knowledge that something vast and patient and hungry was stirring in the dark, and it had been stirring since before Kael was born. Since before his species had learned to split atoms or launch ships beyond their own atmosphere.

He was gasping now. The suit's oxygen readout was irrelevant—he wasn't using air anymore. He was using something else, burning through reserves of consciousness he didn't know he had. His hands were shaking. Both of them. The bare one and the gloved one, trembling in unison like they belonged to something that was coming apart at the seams.

The airlock seemed impossibly far away.

He pushed off from the center of the chamber, and the crystalline structures parted again, creating that same corridor of floating geometry. They seemed to know what he needed before he needed it. Or maybe they were just reacting to the panic that was flowering through his implant, the growing certainty that he had just made a decision that could not be unmade, that had consequences spreading outward like ripples in still water, that would not stop rippling for a very long time.

Seven years. Seven years of telling himself that staying alone, refusing to touch anything, refusing to need anyone would keep them safe. Keep them separate from whatever he carried in his chest like a second heartbeat.

All of it was a lie.

The isolation hadn't protected anyone. It had only delayed the moment when the thing inside him would finally wake up and start broadcasting its hunger across the solar system. It had only postponed the inevitable cascade of failure and death that was already in motion. Already inevitable. Already written into the fundamental architecture of the universe by something that had been dead longer than any human civilization had been alive.

He cycled through the airlock. The pressure equalized. His suit stabilized. And when he looked at his bare hand, floating in the recycled air of the Iron Ghost's airlock, he could have sworn he saw the faintest blue light flickering beneath the skin, pulsing in rhythm with a countdown that only he could hear.

Only he could hear.

Not for long.

The distress signal came through the Iron Ghost's comms at 03:47 ship time, fragmented and high-pitched with panic.

"—mayday, mayday, this is Europa Station, we have multiple system failures, all neural implants reading critical cascade, someone please—"

Static swallowed the rest.

Kael was still in the airlock, his bare hand still glowing faintly with that blue light that shouldn't exist. He heard the signal the way he heard everything now: not through his ears but directly through the device, through the crystalline thing that had made his skull its new home. The signal wasn't just audio. It was data, compressed and screaming, and underneath it ran a frequency that made his teeth ache.

He pulled off his helmet. The recycled air tasted like copper and burnt insulation.

The comms crackled again. A different voice this time, steady and professional, already tipping into the careful detachment that came just before panic: "Europa Research Station to any vessel in range. We are experiencing a critical neural-interface cascade affecting all personnel. Life-support systems are failing. Requesting immediate assistance. Repeat, requesting immediate—"

The voice cut off mid-word. Not static. Not interference. Just silence. The kind of silence that came when every neural implant in a facility went dark at exactly the same time.

Kael moved to the bridge without remembering the journey. His body was following paths it had learned seven years ago, muscle memory that predated thought. His hands found the navigation console. The screen flickered to life under his fingers, and for a moment he saw two images overlapping: the real navigation display and the map that was still burning behind his eyes. The coordinates. The pulsing markers. All of them bright with intention.

Europa was one of them.

The news feeds kicked in three minutes later, the corporate newsfeed with its careful, measured tone: "We are receiving reports of a catastrophic systems failure at Europa Research Station. The Corporate Defense Alliance is investigating. All communication with the facility has ceased as of 03:51. Preliminary analysis suggests a reactor containment breach. Personnel loss is estimated at—"

Estimated at. Everyone. Everyone was estimated at dead.

Kael's hand moved to the communications array. Seven years of discipline, seven years of refusing to call anyone, of keeping the channels dark and the signal quiet. He reached for the transmit button anyway, some animal part of his brain still believing that isolation could be broken if the circumstances were dire enough.

He stopped an inch away from the switch.

If he transmitted, they would hear him. The Corporate Defense Alliance, the megacorp trackers, every hunter with a bounty on his name—they would triangulate his position in minutes. They would come. And they would come knowing that the distress signal from Europa had come right after the device activated. Right after he touched something that shouldn't have been touched.

The coordinates he had seen weren't random locations on a map. They were triggers. Nodes in a network that had been waiting forty thousand years for someone to activate the first one. And he had done it. He had pressed his bare hand against ancient crystalline glass and unlocked something that was supposed to stay locked forever.

His isolation hadn't saved anyone. It had only delayed the inevitable. Delayed the moment when the failsafe would activate, when the signal would spread, when everyone on Europa would feel their neural implants turn to weapons in their own skulls.

Seven years of running. Seven years of telling himself that needing no one meant no one could die because of him. Seven years of believing that a man who refused to lead, refused to trust, refused to touch anything would somehow be protected from the consequences of his own existence.

All of it was a lie so complete that it had become truth.

The silence on the comms stretched on. No more fragmented calls. No more desperate voices. Just the soft hum of dead equipment and the deeper, quieter hum of the device in his chest, pulsing in rhythm with a countdown that had just accelerated beyond all calculation.

Kael turned away from the communications array. He did not transmit. He did not call for help. He did not do anything that might bring rescue or salvation or the illusion that this could still be contained.

Instead, he went to the ship's computer and pulled up the full list of locations the device had shown him. Twenty-three coordinates scattered across the solar system. Twenty-three failsafe nodes, all broadcasting, all counting down to something that had no name in any human language.

One of them had just gone dark.

Twenty-two remained.

He was reaching for the navigation controls when the second distress signal came through—this one from Titan Station. The voice was even more panicked, even more brief. It lasted five seconds before cutting off mid-scream.

Kael didn't move. Didn't reach for the comms. Didn't do anything but watch the lights on his console go dark, one by one, each one representing a location he had seen in that first flood of impossible knowledge. Each one representing hundreds of people whose last moments were being lived right now, in real time, because he had been curious about a beacon that should have been left alone.

The blue light beneath his skin pulsed brighter.

And in the darkness of the Iron Ghost, surrounded by the ghosts of seven years of isolation, Kael Voss finally understood: staying alone didn't save anyone. It only made him the worst possible person to be awake when the world began to end.
